clinicalPearls: The most common inflammatory myopathy of childhood, characterised by proximal muscle weakness together with distinctive skin changes.
Look for the heliotrope rash (violaceous discolouration of the upper eyelids) and Gottron papules over the knuckles, elbows, and knees.
Weakness is typically symmetrical and proximal, so children struggle to climb stairs, rise from the floor, or lift their arms overhead.
Nailfold capillary changes (dilated, dropout, or tortuous loops) are a useful bedside clue and correlate with disease activity.
Calcinosis of skin and soft tissues is a late complication, more likely when treatment is delayed or inadequate.
Unlike adult dermatomyositis, an underlying malignancy is rarely associated in children.
A small vessel vasculopathy can affect the gastrointestinal tract, potentially causing ulceration, bleeding, or perforation.
Early diagnosis and adequate immunosuppression improve outcomes and reduce the risk of chronic disability and calcinosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile dermatomyositis is an immune-mediated systemic vasculopathy affecting small vessels of skeletal muscle, skin, and other organs. Complement-mediated injury to the capillary endothelium leads to capillary dropout, ischaemia, and perifascicular muscle fibre atrophy. Interferon-driven inflammation and immune complex deposition contribute to ongoing muscle and skin damage, producing the characteristic weakness and rash.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic lupus erythematosus / overlap connective tissue disease
Spinal muscular atrophy or other neuromuscular disorders
additionalInvestigations: Serum muscle enzymes (creatine kinase, aldolase, LDH, transaminases)
MRI of muscle to identify inflammation and guide biopsy site
Muscle biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Severe dysphagia or nasal regurgitation indicating pharyngeal muscle involvement with aspiration risk
Respiratory muscle weakness or interstitial lung disease causing hypoventilation
Gastrointestinal vasculopathy with abdominal pain, bleeding, or perforation
Rapidly progressive weakness or inability to protect the airway
Extensive skin ulceration reflecting severe vasculopathy
reference.prognosis: With prompt, adequate immunosuppression many children achieve remission and regain function; delayed or insufficient treatment increases the risk of chronic disease, calcinosis, and long-term disability. A monocyclic course carries the best prognosis.
pitfalls: Attributing subtle proximal weakness to clumsiness or normal fatigue and delaying diagnosis
Assuming normal muscle enzymes exclude the disease, as they can be near-normal in some children
Under-treating early disease and thereby increasing the risk of calcinosis
Overlooking dysphagia and aspiration risk when pharyngeal muscles are involved
